Chapter 3: Ambition, Comedy, and Breaking into Television
You know, dreams usually begin quietly—maybe in the corner of your bedroom, or sitting in the back row of a classroom, just doodling or daydreaming.
If you’ve ever had a knack for making people laugh, you might wonder: could you actually turn your sense of humor into a career? It’s exciting to think about, but let’s be honest, it can also feel totally out of reach. The world of comedy and television seems so far away, packed with big personalities and unwritten rules. Still, ambition has a funny way of sneaking in—maybe after binge-watching late-night reruns, or feeling that rush from landing the perfect punchline.
Once college is over, things get a lot less certain. Suddenly, you’re thinking about rent, groceries, making your parents proud—and at the same time, there’s that persistent itch to do something creative.
If you walk through any big city, you’ll find it’s full of hopefuls, each chasing their own idea of success. Some take temp jobs just to pay the bills, others are waiting tables, answering phones, doing whatever it takes to get by. The days can feel endlessly long, and let’s face it, rejection is everywhere. Auditions that go nowhere, scripts that never get a second glance—and the competition? It’s intense.
But then, every so often, you get this little spark of magic. Maybe it’s a sketch you perform in a tiny theater, and suddenly, the laughter is real and unexpected. Or you meet a writing partner—a collaborator who just gets your sense of humor. Together, you start creating characters and stories that feel both personal and somehow universal. Sure, the process is messy. There are late nights, endless rewrites, moments where you wonder if it’s even worth it. But when it all clicks, it’s exhilarating. Every small win feels like a huge breakthrough.
Trying to break into television? It’s one big lesson in perseverance. The industry’s unpredictable, and chances don’t come around often. Sometimes it’s a random meeting that leads to an audition. Other times, your script floats around for ages before landing in the right hands. There are mentors who step in and offer advice, but there are also gatekeepers—those people who seem determined to keep the doors shut. The trick is learning to be resilient. You’ve got to bounce back from the no’s, keep writing and performing, even if it feels like nobody’s paying attention.
Now, for women in comedy, the challenge can be even bigger. Many rooms are packed with men, and the expectations are different. There’s pressure to be both hilarious and approachable, to stand out but not get labeled as “difficult.” Sometimes, you feel invisible, wondering if anyone even notices you’re there. But humor becomes your shield—a way to handle awkward moments and push back against tired stereotypes. The power to make people laugh? That’s a real kind of strength. It opens doors and forges connections you might never expect.
And slowly, those little victories start to add up. Maybe you land a writing job on a TV show—that leads to even more opportunities. Suddenly, you’re creating and performing your own material. It’s both terrifying and unbelievably rewarding. The work can be relentless—long hours, tight deadlines, constant feedback—but it’s also deeply satisfying. There’s this real sense of belonging, of being on a team that values creativity and collaboration.
Ambition in the creative world? It’s never a straight line. There are setbacks, detours, moments where you question everything—and, just when you least expect it, a flash of inspiration. Hard work, a bit of luck, and the support of friends and mentors all shape the journey. Most people only see the finished product—they miss the years of behind-the-scenes hustle. But if you stick with it, those efforts pay off. The chance to make people laugh, to tell stories that truly connect, that’s a dream absolutely worth chasing.
